sections.section_title: Clinical background and pathobiology: Behçet’s disease, neuro-Behçet’s, and SIADH
sections.description: Build the mechanistic and epidemiologic foundation necessary to interpret this case, focusing on the immunopathology of BD, forms of neuro-BD relevant to aseptic meningitis with normal MRI, and the physiology of ADH and SIADH in CNS inflammation.
subtopics: Behçet’s disease overview: mucocutaneous hallmark lesions, multisystem nature, typical disease course
Immunopathogenesis pertinent to this case: neutrophilic inflammation; Th1/Th17 skew; cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6) and their systemic effects
Neuro-Behçet’s subtypes: parenchymal (brainstem/diencephalon), non-parenchymal (venous sinus thrombosis), and meningoencephalitis/aseptic meningitis presentations
Timing of neuro-BD relative to BD diagnosis and rarity of concurrent onset
ADH regulation and water balance: hypothalamic production, osmoregulation, non-osmotic triggers (nausea, pain, inflammation)
SIADH definition and core diagnostic criteria; common CNS inflammatory triggers
Proposed link between neuroinflammation, IL-6, and dysregulated ADH secretion
HLA-B51: association vs diagnostic utility and why it is not part of international classification criteria

sections.section_title: Presentation and early bedside approach to fever, headache, mucocutaneous lesions, and hyponatraemia
sections.description: Translate the index presentation into an organized initial assessment that prioritizes safety, recognizes pattern-based clues, and sets up targeted investigations.
subtopics: Synthesis of symptoms: fever, headache, vertigo, hiccups, oral/genital aphthae, folliculitis-like rash, arthralgia, malaise
Volume status assessment and recognizing euvolaemic hyponatraemia at the bedside
Hyponatraemia triage: symptom severity, seizure risk, and initial monitoring
Laboratory priorities: serum sodium and osmolality, urine osmolality and sodium, thyroid and adrenal screening, inflammatory markers
Clues to severe hyponatraemia: persistent hiccups and rhabdomyolysis (elevated CK) as often-overlooked manifestations
Early empiric coverage rationale in fever/headache (cefepime; later acyclovir) pending exclusion of CNS infection
Recognizing a BD phenotype during acute evaluation: oral aphthae and later-appearing genital ulcer with folliculitis-like rash

sections.section_title: Diagnostic workup and reasoning: from broad differential to definitive BD, acute neuro-BD, and SIADH
sections.description: Detail the stepwise evaluation, test interpretation, and exclusion of mimics that led to the dual diagnoses and identified SIADH as the cause of hyponatraemia.
subtopics: Key differentials for fever/headache/hyponatraemia: viral and bacterial meningitis/encephalitis, TB meningitis, autoimmune encephalitis, neoplasm (CNS lymphoma), neurosarcoidosis, systemic inflammatory disease
CSF profile in this case: mildly elevated opening pressure, lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein; infectious studies negative—consistent with aseptic meningitis
Neuroimaging nuance: normal MRI does not exclude early neuro-BD or aseptic meningitis; typical neuro-BD predilection sites and why they may be spared
Applying International Criteria for Behçet’s Disease: scoring to ‘definite BD’ based on oral aphthae, genital ulcers, and folliculitis-like rash
Establishing acute neuro-BD: CNS symptoms in the context of definite BD after exclusion of infection, neoplasm, and other autoimmune etiologies
Interpreting ancillary tests: limited utility of ACE, sIL-2R, and HLA-B51 in this diagnostic context; avoiding indiscriminate testing

Diagnosing SIADH: hypotonic hyponatraemia with inappropriately concentrated urine and elevated urine sodium, clinical euvolaemia, normal thyroid/adrenal function; elevated ADH level as supportive but not required
Linking the entities: temporal association of neuroinflammation and SIADH; plausible IL-6–mediated ADH dysregulation

sections.section_title: Management strategy: treating acute neuro-BD and controlling SIADH safely
sections.description: Explain therapeutic decision-making, including standard-of-care options versus the chosen approach, safe sodium correction practices, and multidisciplinary supportive care.
subtopics: Empiric antimicrobials and antivirals: indications to start and clear criteria to de-escalate once infections are excluded
Standard therapy for acute neuro-BD: typical first-line high-dose corticosteroids; roles for azathioprine, methotrexate, cyclophosphamide, and TNF inhibitors when needed
Colchicine in BD: mechanism (neutrophil inhibition; cytokine modulation) and usual indications for mucocutaneous disease; evidence gap for neuro-BD and rationale for trial in this patient
Contextualizing steroid-sparing choice: glycaemic concerns and mild, non-focal neuro presentation

SIADH management principles: fluid restriction targets, sodium correction limits per 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination, indications for hypertonic saline or vasopressin antagonists, and close electrolyte monitoring
Topical therapies for mucocutaneous lesions and supportive care
Co-morbidity management: timing of diabetes therapy optimization and rehabilitation for deconditioning
Monitoring response: clinical improvement, normalization of sodium and ADH, inflammatory markers, and re-assessment triggers

sections.description: Summarize the patient’s course and distill practical takeaways, emphasizing vigilance for SIADH in neuroinflammation, cautious test selection, and follow-up strategies for BD/neuro-BD.
subtopics: Clinical course: rapid improvement after colchicine; normalization of sodium and ADH; resolution of mucocutaneous and neurological symptoms
Long-term outcome: sustained remission on colchicine monotherapy and subsequent safe diabetes management
When to suspect acute neuro-BD in BD patients: non-specific CNS symptoms plus hyponatraemia, even with normal MRI
Teaching points on diagnostics: MRI can be normal early; BD diagnosis is clinical; interpret ACE and sIL-2R cautiously; HLA-B51 is supportive, not diagnostic
Recognizing SIADH manifestations: hiccups and rhabdomyolysis as hyponatraemia clues in CNS inflammation
Evidence and gaps: plausibility of IL-6–mediated SIADH in neuro-BD vs non-specific response to CNS inflammation; need for further data
Follow-up plan: relapse surveillance for neuro-BD, ophthalmologic checks, cardiovascular risk management, triggers for re-imaging or CSF analysis, and coordination between neurology and rheumatology
